summary30s: The Permanent Settlement was enacted in Bengal in 1793 under Governor-General Lord Cornwallis, fixing revenue demands on Zamindars in perpetuity.
Zamindars frequently defaulted due to exorbitant initial revenue rates and the 'Sunset Law', giving rise to wealthy village-based peasants called 'Jotedars'.

In the Rajmahal hills, British authorities clashed with the hill-dwelling Paharias (represented by the 'Hoe'), and settled the agricultural Santhals (represented by the 'Plough') in Damin-i-Koh in 1832.
Exploited by moneylenders (Dikus) and British taxes, Santhals rebelled in 1855-56 under brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Manjhi, leading to the creation of the Santhal Pargana.

In the Bombay Deccan, the Ryotwari system and the end of the American Civil War Cotton Boom led to crushing peasant debt; the 1875 Deccan Riots against moneylenders produced the 1878 Deccan Riots Report.

coreConcepts.title: The Permanent Settlement (1793) and the Rise of Jotedars
coreConcepts.explanation: Introduced in Bengal in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis, the Permanent Settlement fixed the land revenue payable by Zamindars forever. If a Zamindar failed to pay by sunset on a specified date (the 'Sunset Law'), his estate was liable to be auctioned. Over 75% of zamindaris changed hands after 1793. Why did Zamindars default? (1) The initial revenue demand was pegged exorbitantly high; (2) Agricultural prices were depressed in the 1790s; (3) The revenue was invariable regardless of harvest failure; (4) The Company curbed zamindars' police power and judicial autonomy. Concurrently, a class of rich peasants known as 'Jotedars' (also termed haoladars, gantidars, or mandals) consolidated power in North Bengal. Jotedars controlled local trade and moneylending, directly resisted zamindars, and deliberately delayed revenue payments.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part III, Section 1: 'Bengal and the Zamindars'
coreConcepts.examTip: Fifth Report: Submitted to the British Parliament in 1813 by a Select Committee on the affairs of the East India Company, running into 1,002 pages, documenting the crisis of Bengal zamindars.

coreConcepts.title: The Hoe and the Plough: Paharias vs Santhals
coreConcepts.explanation: In the Rajmahal hills, the indigenous Paharias lived by shifting agriculture, forest produce (Mahua flowers, silk cocoons), and charcoal burning, symbolized by the 'Hoe'. Francis Buchanan, a physician/surveyor who toured the region in the early 19th century, observed their distrust of British officials. When British efforts to tame Paharias failed, the British turned to the Santhals, who practiced settled plough agriculture (symbolized by the 'Plough'). By 1832, a large area of land in the foothills was demarcated as 'Damin-i-Koh' (the skirts of the hills) and declared the land of the Santhals. Santhal population and villages expanded rapidly.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part III, Section 2: 'The Hoe and the Plough'
coreConcepts.examTip: Hoe = Paharias (shifting cultivation, forest dwellers); Plough = Santhals (settled agriculture, clearing forests).

coreConcepts.title: The Santhal Rebellion of 1855-56
coreConcepts.explanation: Santhals soon discovered that the land demarcated for them was slipping out of their grasp. The colonial state levied heavy land taxes, zamindars asserted control over the Damin-i-Koh tracts, and moneylenders ('Dikus') charged usurious interest rates (often 50% to 500%), reducing peasants to bonded laborers. In 1855, Santhals rose in armed rebellion under the leadership of two brothers, Sidhu and Kanhu Manjhi. Armed with bows, arrows, and battle-axes, they attacked zamindars, moneylenders, and police stations. The British suppressed the insurrection ruthlessly through martial law, burning villages. Following the revolt, the British carved out the 'Santhal Pargana' (5,500 square miles) from Bhagalpur and Birbhum to conciliate the tribals.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part III, Section 2
coreConcepts.examTip: Leaders of the 1855-56 Santhal revolt: Sidhu and Kanhu Manjhi.

coreConcepts.title: The Deccan Riots (1875) and the Limitation Law
coreConcepts.explanation: In Bombay Deccan, the British implemented the Ryotwari settlement: revenue was settled directly with the ryot (cultivator), not permanently, but revised upwards every 30 years. During the American Civil War (1861-65), Britain turned to India for raw cotton, creating an artificial 'Cotton Boom'. Moneylenders (sahukars) gave easy credit to ryots. When the American Civil War ended in 1865, demand collapsed, cotton prices plummeted by 50%, and moneylenders refused further loans while the colonial state hiked revenue by 50%. The British passed the 'Limitation Law of 1859', stating that loan bonds signed between moneylenders and ryots were valid for only three years; moneylenders manipulated this by forcing peasants to sign new bonds every three years, compounding unpaid interest. In May 1875, riots erupted at Supa (Poona district), where ryots attacked sahukars, publicly burning debt bonds (khatas). The Deccan Riots Commission presented its report to the British Parliament in 1878.
coreConcepts.ncertPointer: Themes in Indian History Part III, Sections 3 & 4
coreConcepts.examTip: The Limitation Law of 1859 set loan bond validity to 3 years, which moneylenders exploited to compound interest.

workedExamples.question:
Which of the following British legal enactments, passed in 1859, declared that loan bonds signed between moneylenders and ryots would have validity for only three years?
(A) Sunset Law
(B) Limitation Law
(C) Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act
(D) Vernacular Press Act
workedExamples.explanation: In 1859 the British passed a Limitation Law that stated that the loan bonds signed between moneylenders and ryots would have validity for only three years. Its objective was to curb accumulation of interest, but moneylenders circumvented it by compelling peasants to sign new bonds every three years.
solutionStepByStep: Step 1: Sunset Law (1793) -> Associated with Bengal Permanent Settlement zamindari auctions.
Step 2: Limitation Law (1859) -> Passed in Bombay Deccan; limited bond validity to 3 years.
Step 3: Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act (1879) -> Passed after the Deccan Riots report.
Conclusion: Option B (Limitation Law) is correct.

commonTraps.misconception: Thinking the Ryotwari settlement in Bombay fixed revenue permanently like Bengal.
commonTraps.correctConcept: Ryotwari revenue was NOT permanent. It was subject to upward revision every 30 years based on fresh land surveys and soil classification.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Students confuse Permanent Settlement (Bengal) with Ryotwari (Bombay/Madras).
commonTraps.cuetWarning: Permanent = Bengal only; Ryotwari = Revised every 30 years.

commonTraps.misconception: Believing Jotedars were loyal agents of the Zamindar.
commonTraps.correctConcept: Jotedars were bitter rivals of the Zamindar. They lived in the village, mobilized the ryots, delayed revenue payments to bankrupt the Zamindar, and bought his auctioned estates.
commonTraps.whyTrapWorks: Questions suggest Jotedars collected taxes for the Zamindar.

practiceQuestions.question: Who was the Governor-General of Bengal when the Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Permanent Settlement was made with the rajas and taluqdars of Bengal in 1793 under Governor-General Lord Cornwallis.

practiceQuestions.question: Under the Permanent Settlement, what was the 'Sunset Law'?

options.text: No court hearings could occur after sunset
If revenue was not paid by sunset of the specified due date, the zamindari estate was auctioned
Cultivators had to cease all agricultural operations at sunset
British collectors could only enter villages before sunset

practiceQuestions.explanation: According to the Sunset Law, if payment did not come in by sunset of the specified day, the zamindari was liable to be auctioned.

practiceQuestions.question: In which year was 'Damin-i-Koh' demarcated as a separate territory for the Santhals in the Rajmahal hills?
practiceQuestions.explanation: By 1832 a large area of land was demarcated as Damin-i-Koh, declared to be the land of the Santhals.

practiceQuestions.question: Which physician and surveyor travelled through the Rajmahal hills in the early 19th century, leaving detailed accounts of Paharias and Santhals?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Francis Buchanan (later Buchanan-Hamilton) was a surgeon and surveyor employed by the East India Company who surveyed Rajmahal hills.

practiceQuestions.question: Where did the Deccan Riots of May 1875 first break out in Maharashtra?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The movement began at Supa, a large village in Poona (Pune) district, which was a market center where many shopkeepers and moneylenders lived.

practiceQuestions.question: What was the main action taken by rioting ryots during the Deccan Riots of 1875?

options.text: Burning debt bonds, loan agreements, and account books (khatas)
Blowing up railway bridges and telegraph lines
Refusing to cultivate any food crops

practiceQuestions.explanation: The ryots attacked the moneylenders, burning the bahi-khatas (account books) and debt bonds in public bonfires.

practiceQuestions.question: Which war in the West created an unprecedented boom in Indian raw cotton exports between 1861 and 1865?
practiceQuestions.explanation: When the American Civil War broke out in 1861, cotton supply from America to Britain plummeted, causing Britain to look to India for raw cotton.

practiceQuestions.question: What was the famous parliamentary report on East India Company administration submitted in Britain in 1813 called?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Fifth Report was submitted to the British Parliament in 1813 on the administration and activities of the East India Company in India.

practiceQuestions.question: Rich peasants who were called 'Jotedars' in Dinajpur (North Bengal) were known by which of the following terms in other parts of Bengal?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In some places they were called haoladars, elsewhere they were known as gantidars or mandals.

practiceQuestions.question:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R):
Assertion (A): The British welcomed the settlement of Santhals in the foothills of Rajmahal.
Reason (R): The British failed to subdue the shifting-cultivator Paharias into settled tax-paying peasants, whereas Santhals were skilled in clearing forests and practicing plough agriculture.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)

practiceQuestions.explanation: Having failed to tame the Paharias, the British turned to Santhals, who appeared ideal to clear forests and settle the land. Both are true and (R) explains (A).
